title: Atomic-scale composition of the ternary III-V semiconductor (Al,Ga)Sb visualized by cross-sectional scanning tunneling microscopy
authors: Hitesh Kumar, Vladimir Kaganer, Zijin Lei, Rüdiger Schott, Werner Wegscheider, Stefan Fölsch
abstract: Cross-sectional scanning tunneling microscopy at 5 K is used to investigate cation mixing in (Al,Ga)Sb layers grown by molecular beam epitaxy, via direct atom counting at the (1-10) and (110) cleavage planes. Electronic contrast between Al and Ga surface cations enables statistical analysis of the metal sublattice along the non-equivalent <110> directions within the zincblende (001) surface and along the [001] growth direction. The cation distribution is found to be random both along the growth direction and within the growth plane, with no evidence of long-range order or anisotropic growth kinetics; notably, the mean numbers of consecutive cations of the same type along the two in-plane directions are equal, possibly due to statistical averaging over randomly distributed subsurface cations. The results are compatible with either strain-mediated interactions during cation incorporation at the growth front or ideal, uncorrelated cation mixing. Overall, the examined (Al,Ga)Sb alloy shows an exceptionally high degree of atomic-level homogeneity.
summary: This work uses cross-sectional STM to examine the atomic arrangement in (Al,Ga)Sb semiconductors. By directly counting atoms and analyzing electronic contrast, the researchers determined that the cation mixing is statistically random. This finding suggests the material possesses remarkable atomic-level homogeneity, consistent with either ideal mixing or weak, non-anisotropic interactions.
main_problem: The study investigates the atomic-scale composition and cation mixing behavior within the ternary III-V semiconductor (Al,Ga)Sb.
main_result: The cation distribution was found to be statistically random both along the growth direction and within the growth plane, indicating an exceptionally high degree of atomic-level homogeneity.
method: Cross-sectional Scanning Tunneling Microscopy (XSTM) was employed at 5 K, utilizing electronic contrast to perform direct atom counting on cleaved surfaces.
model_or_system: The physical system is the (Al,Ga)Sb alloy grown by Molecular Beam Epitaxy (MBE). Analysis involves comparing experimental cation statistics against theoretical models, such as random occupancy or Markov-chain models accounting for strain-mediated interactions.
key_observables: Cation distribution statistics (randomness vs. correlation), mean number of consecutive cations of the same type ($\langle n angle$), and electronic contrast between Al and Ga surface cations.
important_parameters: Temperature (5 K), semiconductor composition (Al/Ga ratio), and crystallographic directions ($\langle 110 angle$, $[001]$).
main_assumptions: The observed contrast is attributed to electronic differences (dangling-bond states) between Al and Ga atoms, and that statistical averaging over subsurface cations restores isotropy.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the relative orientations of cleavage planes, show cross-sections revealing chemical contrast between Al and Ga, and compare measured mean cation lengths ($\langle n angle$) against theoretical predictions from random and correlated models.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by detailing the experimental setup (XSTM on specific planes), presenting the direct atom counting results, developing theoretical models (random vs. correlated mixing), and concluding by comparing the measured statistics against these models to establish the degree of homogeneity.
why_interesting: While primarily materials science, the analysis of local atomic order and the comparison to theoretical models (random vs. correlated) touches upon concepts of quenched disorder and local energy minimization, which are relevant to understanding complex many-body systems.
